The intricate life cycle of Horseshoe worm (Phoronis pallida) begins with the fertilised ovum entering a brief embryonated egg phase. Under culture conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the absolute age at first feeding is approximately 2 days [ab = approximately 2 days]. This rapid developmental progression reflects the relatively small investment per offspring, as the wet weight at birth is an exceedingly modest 0.00000011 grams [Wwb = 0.00000011 grams]. This minute mass corresponds to a minute oocyte diameter that yields minimal yolk reserves, compelling the newly emerged larva to commence exogenous feeding almost immediately. The swift transition from embryonated egg to planktonic larva is characteristic of phoronids, which produce large numbers of small offspring to exploit patchy food resources in the water column.

Following a period of active growth, the free-swimming larva of Phoronis pallida undergoes a dramatic metamorphic climax to become a post-metamorphic juvenile. Once settled, the juvenile enters a phase of rapid somatic expansion that eventually leads to the reproductively active adult stage. Under laboratory conditions, the maximum recorded adult body length is 14 centimeters [Li = 14 centimeters], placing this species among the larger members of its phylum. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown individual is 0.11 grams [Wwi = 0.11 grams], a value that is derived from the product of the body length and cross-sectional area, assuming a typical adult trunk diameter of approximately one millimeter as documented by Emig. This slender, elongated morphology enables the worm to occupy narrow, cryptic crevices within its preferred substrate.

Reproductive timing in Phoronis pallida is tightly coupled to thermal conditions. In a laboratory setting maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], individuals attain sexual maturity after a specific interval from birth; the time since birth at puberty is documented as 200 days [tp = 200 days]. This relatively protracted juvenile phase likely reflects the energetic demands of constructing the characteristic lophophore apparatus and achieving the body size necessary for successful gametogenesis. The onset of gonadal activity marks a major physiological transition, after which energy allocation shifts toward the production of gametes. This timing is consistent with the broadly iteroparous reproductive strategy observed among phoronid worms, where repeated spawning events occur over an extended breeding season following the achievement of maturity.

The lifespan of Phoronis pallida further illustrates its life-history strategy. When reared in stable aquarium conditions at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum recorded longevity reaches 365 days [am = 365 days]. This one-year lifespan is relatively short compared to some longer-lived lophophorates, yet it is sufficient to encompass multiple reproductive bouts given the relatively early age at puberty described earlier. The coupling of a moderate lifespan with a relatively early onset of reproduction is typical of species that experience high adult mortality rates in the field, favoring an efficient schedule of early and repeated reproductive effort. The eventual senescence is characterized by progressive physiological deterioration, culminating in organismal death after the completion of the annual life cycle.

Reproductive output in Phoronis pallida has been quantified under controlled temperatures. Spawning females produce approximately 28 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 28 eggs per clutch], and they can generate up to 2 to 3 clutches each year [F_R_i = up to 2 to 3 clutches each year] when maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This high annual frequency of spawning events compensates for the modest clutch size, resulting in a substantial total fecundity over the course of the reproductive season. The year-round availability of suitable planktonic food in the laboratory setting likely supports this continuous reproductive schedule, though field data suggest that natural populations may exhibit more pronounced seasonality linked to phytoplankton blooms. The capacity for repeated spawning underscores the opportunistic life-history strategy of this species.
